newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Fraud alleged as Armenia elects new president.
newsitem.headline: Fraud alleged as Armenia elects new president.

text.p: Armenians held a presidential election on Sunday dominated by bitter rivalry between President Ter Petrosyan and his former prime minister, Vazgen Manukyan.

Manukyan and his party, the National Democratic Union (NDU) alleged serious irregularities during the course of voting, and an international monitor said he had witnessed fraud committed in favor of Ter-Petrosyan.
"There are rather strong abuses going on. We are expecting them to get worse tonight when they start counting the ballots," Manukyan told Reuters in front of his headquarters.

An NDU official said the infractions included ballot box stuffing by Ter-Petrosyan supporters. He claimed police and precinct officials were intimidating people into voting for Ter-Petrosyan by watching them mark ballot papers, and that Manukyan vote monitors were forced out of some polling places.

The charges could not be confirmed, but one international monitor said that he had observed Armenian regular soldiers being ordered by commanding officiers to vote for Ter-Petrosyan and engaging in multiple voting.

"The officer was telling them how to mark the ballots, then the whole unit was taken to another precinct where they voted a second time," said the monitor, adding that it was early to say if the infractions threatened the legitimacy of the election.
Polling places visited by this correspondent were calm and officials and voters reported no problems.

Ter-Petrosyan has led the country through a time of acute economic hardship caused partly by a protracted confrontation with neighbouring Azerbaijan over its largely-Armenian enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh.
Voters in the mountainous Caucasus state of 3.5 million sandwiched between Iran, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey had until 10 p.m.(1800 GMT) to cast ballots.
The Central Elections Commission said that 36.5 percent of of the 2.21 million electorate had turned up by five p.m. (1300 GMT). The flow of voters in Yerevan visibly increased in the evening hours.
Out of four candidates, only Ter-Petrosyan, a sometimes aloof academic running for a second and final five years in office, and Manukyan have a realistic chance of winning.
If no candidate wins more than 50 percent of the votes cast, a second round runoff will be held in two weeks.
Ter-Petrosyan, 51, casting his ballot in central Yerevan, said he was "very encouraged" by his chances and hailed the vote as a milestone in establishing Armenia as a democratic state.

Manukyan, 50, who has made sweeping promises to raise living standards quickly in the impoverished country, predicted victory as he voted at a polling station in the Armenian Writers' Union in the early morning.
The contest between the two former close allies, both of whom played big roles in leading Armenia to independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, has become bitter.
Ter-Petrosyan has made few promises, focusing on stability, recent economic progress and victories over neighbouring Azerbaijan in an eight-year war over territory.
But sensing his rival gaining ground, he launched blistering attacks in the closing hours of the campaign saying that a Manukyan presidency would bring "tyranny and chaos".
Manukyan has pledged to revive industry and improve the lot of the average person, still hurting from economic collapse brought on by the war and the demise of the Soviet union.
Most people are still poor but the economy has begun to recover.

Also on the ballot are Communist Sergei Badalyan and Ashot Manucharyan of the Scientific-Industrial Citizens Union. Manucharyan has practically given up his candidacy and his campaign backers have been telling voters to vote for Manukyan.
If no candidate gets 50 percent of the vote, a second round will be held in two weeks between the two frontrunners.
The electoral commission said that first returns from voting could not be expected before Monday morning.
